title: Physics 1: Mechanics
subject: Mechanics
summary: Calculus-based Newtonian mechanics, from kinematics and Newton's laws through energy, momentum, rotation, gravitation, oscillations and a brief look at fluids. Builds the problem-solving habits (free-body diagrams, conservation laws, limiting-case checks) needed for every later course; chemistry hooks include potential-energy curves, reduced mass, moments of inertia and damped resonance.

units.title: Units, Estimation & Vectors
units.summary: The working toolkit for every later lesson: units, dimensional analysis, order-of-magnitude estimates and vector algebra (dot and cross products); the chemist's unit-conversion habits carry over directly.

lessons.title: Unit Conversion & Dimensional Analysis
objectives: Convert between SI and other unit systems by chaining conversion factors, and check a result's units at every step.
Use dimensional analysis to test whether a formula can be correct and to guess the form of a relation such as T ~ sqrt(l/g).

lectures.title: Lecture 1: Powers of 10, Units, Dimensions, Uncertainties, Scaling Arguments (dimensional analysis and the falling-apple test)

lessons.title: Fermi Estimates & Significant Figures
objectives: Make a Fermi estimate of an unfamiliar quantity (e.g. molecules in a breath of air) by decomposing it into factors good to a power of ten.
Report an answer with an appropriate number of significant figures and state when a result is only good to an order of magnitude.

objectives: Compute the scalar product from components and from magnitudes and angle, and use it to find the angle between two vectors and the projection of one on another.

objectives: Compute the vector product from the determinant (component) form and state its direction via the right-hand rule.
Explain why the cross product is anticommutative (and obeys the right-hand rule) and what its magnitude measures geometrically (parallelogram area).
Recognise the cross product in physics: torque as r x F, and later angular momentum as r x p and the magnetic force q v x B.

units.title: Kinematics
units.summary: Describing motion without asking why: position, velocity and acceleration as derivatives and integrals, constant-acceleration formulas, projectiles, circular motion and relative velocity.

objectives: State Kepler's three laws and identify which depends on angular-momentum conservation (equal areas) and which on the inverse-square law (T^2 proportional to a^3).
Derive Kepler's third law for a circular orbit and apply it to planets, moons and binary stars.
Use the ellipse parameters (a, e, perihelion, aphelion) to compute speeds with energy and angular-momentum conservation.

lessons.title: Tidal Forces
objectives: Explain tidal forces as the gradient of the gravitational field: the differential pull across an extended body.
Estimate the tidal acceleration across the Earth due to the Moon, delta g about 2GMR/d^3, and explain the two bulges and spring and neap tides.

lessons.title: Simple Harmonic Motion: Equation, Solution & Circular Projection
objectives: Derive the equation of motion x'' = -omega^2 x for a mass on a spring and write the general solution x = A cos(omega t + phi).
Extract amplitude, phase, period and frequency from initial conditions or a graph.
Relate SHM to a projection of uniform circular motion.

Compute the vibrational frequency of a diatomic from k and reduced mass and connect to IR spectroscopy (wavenumber).

Estimate the error of the small-angle approximation and describe how the period grows with amplitude.

Compute the period of a torsional pendulum, T = 2 pi sqrt(I/kappa), and explain what plays the role of the spring constant.
